summary: Gives an overview of the Handle System, a general-purpose global name service for secured name resolution and administration. It describes the namespace and service architecture and the relationship to DNS, LDAP/X.500 and URNs. Handles are unique names for digital objects and other Internet resources. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3650 describes the Handle System, a global naming service built at CNRI. A handle is two parts, a naming authority and a local name, such as 10.1045/january99-bearman. The values stored against a handle can change without the handle changing, so a name keeps working when the thing it names moves. A central registry tells clients which service holds each authority.

questions: why is the handle system different from dns
what is a naming authority in the handle system
subtitle: An overview of a name service that gives digital objects a name that survives when they move

tldr.problem: Names such as web addresses are tied to where the thing they name happens to live, so moving it, or selling it, breaks the name. DNS was not built to be a general naming service either, since its administration sits with the network administrator.
tldr.mechanism: The Handle System gives every object a handle, a naming authority followed by a slash and a local name. A Global Handle Registry points clients at the Local Handle Service that holds each naming authority, and any handle can carry several values, each with its own access control and its own administrators.
tldr.outcome: The handle stays the same while its values change, so the name persists across moves. The memo notes that the IETF has never reached consensus on how the Handle System fits into the IETF's own architecture for identifiers, and that some of its characterisations of existing systems do not match that consensus.

facts.label: Handle format
facts.value: Naming authority, a slash, then the local name

facts.label: Top-level service
facts.value: One Global Handle Registry, plus any number of Local Handle Services

today: RFC 3650 is an Informational memo from November 2003 that has not been obsoleted or updated. It carries an IESG note that the IETF and IRTF discussions of the Handle System never produced IETF consensus on it or on how it fits into the IETF architecture for identifiers, and that its characterisations of existing systems may not match the IETF consensus view. The memo records that the Handle System was conceived and developed at CNRI, with the first public implementation created there in the fall of 1994, and that early adopters included the Library of Congress, the Defense Technical Information Center and the International DOI Foundation.

sections.title: What the Handle System Is
sections.content:
The Handle System is a distributed information system designed to provide an efficient, extensible and secured global name service for use on networks such as the Internet. It includes an open protocol, a namespace and a reference implementation. The protocol lets a distributed computer system store the names, or handles, of digital resources and resolve those handles into the information needed to locate, access and otherwise use the resources. Those associated values can be changed as needed to reflect the current state of the identified resource without changing the handle, so the name of an item persists over changes of location and other state information. Each handle may have its own administrators, and administration can be done in a distributed environment.

The Handle System provides a confederated name service that lets any existing local namespace join the global handle namespace by obtaining a unique Handle System naming authority. Local names and their value bindings remain intact after joining, and any handle request to the local namespace may be processed by a service interface speaking the Handle System protocol. Combined with the unique naming authority, any local name is guaranteed unique under the global handle namespace.

The design objectives are stated as a list. Uniqueness: every handle is globally unique within the Handle System. Persistence: handles may be used as persistent identifiers, and a handle does not have to be derived from the entity it names, so the same name can persist over changes of location and ownership. Multiple instances: a single handle can refer to several instances of a resource at different and possibly changing locations, so a service can distribute its load. Multiple attributes: a single handle can refer to several attributes of a resource, including associated services. Extensible namespace: existing local namespaces may join by acquiring a unique naming authority. International support: the namespace is based on Unicode 3.0, which includes most characters currently used around the world, and the protocol mandates UTF-8 as the encoding for handles. Distributed service model: any local namespace may be serviced by a local handle service, by the global service, or by both. Secured name service: standard mechanisms for client and server authentication and service authorisation, with options for data integrity and confidentiality. Distributed administration: each handle may define its own administrators, so it can be managed securely over the public network from any location. Efficient resolution: separate service interfaces may be defined for name resolution and administration, so that the cost of administration does not slow resolution.
sections.plainLanguage: A handle is a name that points at a set of values rather than at a place. Move the thing and you change the values; the handle stays the same and still works. That is the whole idea, and the rest of the memo is about how the names are organised and how they are protected.

sections.title: The Handle Namespace
sections.content:
Every handle consists of two parts: its naming authority, otherwise known as its prefix, and a unique local name under that naming authority, otherwise known as its suffix. The two are separated by the ASCII character '/'. The collection of local names under a naming authority defines the local handle namespace for that authority, and any local name must be unique under its local namespace. The uniqueness of a naming authority and of a local name under that authority ensures that any handle is globally unique within the Handle System.

For example, 10.1045/january99-bearman is a handle for an article published in D-Lib magazine, with naming authority 10.1045 and local name january99-bearman. The handle namespace can be considered a superset of many local namespaces, each with a unique naming authority. The naming authority identifies the administrative unit of creation, although not necessarily of continuing administration, of the associated handles.

Naming authorities are defined in a hierarchical fashion resembling a tree structure. Each node and leaf of the tree is given a label corresponding to a naming authority segment, and the parent node notifies the parent naming authority of its child nodes. Unlike DNS, handle naming authorities are constructed left to right, concatenating the labels from the root of the tree to the node that represents the naming authority, with each label separated by the octet used for the ASCII character '.'. A naming authority for the National Digital Library Program, ndlp, at the Library of Congress, loc, is defined as loc.ndlp. Any child naming authority can only be registered by its parent after the parent has been registered, but there is no intrinsic administrative relationship between the namespaces represented by the parent and child naming authorities: they may be served by different handle services, and they may or may not share any administration privileges.

Handles may consist of any printable characters from the Universal Character Set UCS-2 of ISO/IEC 10646, which is exactly the character set defined by Unicode version 3.0. To allow compatibility with existing systems and prevent ambiguity among different encodings, the protocol mandates UTF-8 as the only encoding used for handles, and UTF-8 preserves any ASCII encoded names so that existing names can be used without causing a naming conflict. By default handles are case sensitive, but any individual handle service may define its namespace so that ASCII characters within any handle under that namespace are case insensitive.
sections.plainLanguage: A handle reads like 10.1045/january99-bearman: a prefix that says who is in charge, and a name that is unique within their part of the world. The prefix itself is built up in pieces, left to right, so loc.ndlp means ndlp under loc.

sections.title: The Service Architecture
sections.content:
The Handle System defines a hierarchical service model. The top level is a single handle service, the Global Handle Registry. The lower level consists of all other handle services, known as Local Handle Services. The Global Handle Registry can manage any handle namespace, and is unique among handle services only in that it provides the service used to manage naming authorities, all of which are managed as handles. The naming authority handle holds the information that clients use to reach the local handle service for handles under that authority. Local Handle Services are intended to be hosted by organisations with administrative responsibility for handles under certain naming authorities, and each one must be registered with the Global Handle Registry.

The architecture is distributed. Each handle service may consist of one or more service sites, and each service site is a complete replication of every other site in the service in terms of handle resolution. A site may consist of one or more handle servers, and all handles directed at a given site are evenly distributed across those servers. There are no design limits on the number of services, sites or servers, and replication among sites does not require that each site contain the same number of servers. This is intended to aid scalability, accommodate any large scale of operation and mitigate single points of failure.

Each handle service manages a distinct sub-namespace, and namespaces under different handle services may not overlap. The service is called the home service of the naming authorities it holds, and it is the only one that provides resolution and administration for handles under them. Before resolving a handle, a client has to determine its home service, which is the home service of the handle's naming authority and is registered at the Global Handle Registry. The registry maintains naming authority handles, each of which holds service information describing the home service: its service sites and the interface to each handle server within each site.

The memo gives a worked example. A client resolving 10.1045/july95-arms first queries the Global Handle Registry for the naming authority handle 10.1045, the registry returns the service information of the Local Handle Service responsible for that authority, and the client then uses that information to ask the Local Handle Service for the handle's values. Any client may cache the service information from the registry, and a separate handle caching server, stand-alone or part of a general caching mechanism, may provide shared caching within a local community. With a cached resolution result, subsequent queries of the same handle can be answered locally without contacting any handle service.
sections.plainLanguage: There is one registry at the top and many local services below it. A client asks the registry which service holds a given prefix, then asks that service for the values. Every step can be cached, so repeat lookups are quick.

sections.title: Securing Resolution and Administration
sections.content:
Each handle can be assigned a set of values, and clients use the resolution service to resolve a handle into its values. Each value has a data type and a unique value index, and clients can query for specific values by type or index. The administration service answers requests to manage handles: adding handles, deleting them or updating their values. It also manages naming authorities through naming authority handles. Each handle can have its own administrators, and each administrator can be granted a certain set of permissions. The authentication protocol authenticates the handle administrator before any administrative request is fulfilled.

The system provides client and server authentication, data confidentiality and integrity, and non-repudiation. By default, handle resolution does not require any client authentication. Resolution requests for confidential data assigned to a handle by its administrator, and any administration requests, do require authentication of the client, and the server decides during the authorisation process whether the client may read those values or may add or update handles and values. When authentication is required the handle server issues a challenge to the client, and the client must send back the correct response identifying itself as a qualified administrator before the server responds to the request.

Handle clients may use either secret key or public key cryptography for authentication, and authentication can also be carried out through third party authentication services. To ensure data integrity, clients may request digitally signed responses from any handle server, and they may set up secured communication sessions so that exchanged information can be encrypted with a session key. Handle servers can also provide confidentiality by encrypting the handle data before sending it to the client.

The memo is careful about what this does not buy. The service options for secured information exchange do not guarantee the truthfulness of handle values: incorrect values assigned by an administrator may well mislead clients. A handle value may, however, contain references to other handle values to provide additional credentials, so a value carrying a claim can point at another value holding a digital signature from a creditable source, and clients who trust the signature can then trust the claim.
sections.plainLanguage: Reading a handle is open by default, but changing one, or reading values the administrator marked private, needs a password or a key. What the system cannot do is tell you the values are true: it protects the channel and the administrator's identity, not the truth of the claim.

sections.title: Handles Beside DNS, LDAP and URNs
sections.content:
The memo compares the Handle System with the other naming services of the Internet. DNS was designed and is heavily used for mapping domain names into IP addresses for routing, and the growth of the Internet has raised demands for extensions to it, including possible use as a general-purpose resource naming system. However, such use has the potential to slow down address translation and affect its effectiveness in routing, and DNS implementations do not scale well when a large amount of data is associated with a particular name, so it is generally considered inappropriate to use DNS as a general-purpose naming service. The DNS administrative model argues against it too: names are managed at the zone level by the network administrators, with no provision for per-name administrative structure and no facilities for anyone other than the network administrator to create or manage DNS names.

X.500 is the OSI Directory Standard, designed to provide a white pages service returning telephone numbers or X.400 addresses of people. It defines a hierarchical data and information model with protocols for global name lookup and search, but the protocol has proved difficult to implement and there has been difficulty getting client access integrated into existing products. LDAP has overcome many of these difficulties by making the protocol simpler, though some concern remains as LDAP emerges from a local directory access protocol into a distributed service protocol. The fundamental difference between a name resolution service such as the Handle System and a directory service such as LDAP is search capability: the added functionality of searching necessarily carries added complexity and affects efficiency. A pure name service can be designed solely around efficient resolution of known items, without the data structures needed for discovery of unknown items from incomplete criteria. Directory services may be used in tandem with the Handle System to provide reverse lookup, and handles could be used in LDAP service referral, so that a reference to an LDAP service remains valid when it moves.

URI defines a uniform naming mechanism for identifying Internet resources in web applications, and URN is a subset of URI that defines a namespace registration mechanism for persistent namespaces. Like DNS or X.500, the Handle System defines its namespace outside any URI or URN namespace, and handles can be transcribed and resolved directly without any scheme as a prefix. Applications may still define their own URI or URN namespace and use handles underneath, in the same way that different URI schemes such as telnet, ftp and mailto all use the DNS service. The IETF and IRTF have discussed the Handle System in the realm of URI-related work, with different opinions on whether it fits into a specific URI or URN namespace; those discussions are out of the scope of the document.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS is built for turning names into addresses and is managed zone by zone by network staff. LDAP is built for searching, which is powerful but slow. Handles do neither: they only resolve a name you already know, and they leave naming to whoever owns the thing named.

sections.title: Security Considerations in Practice
sections.content:
The security of the Handle System depends on both client and server host security at every step in a transaction. It assumes the client host has not been tampered with and that client software will reliably convey received data. Trusting the Global Handle Registry means believing that it will correctly direct the client request to the responsible Local Handle Service, and trusting a Local Handle Service means believing it will correctly return the data assigned by the administrator, and therefore implies trusting the naming authorities it supports. The integrity of the system depends heavily on the integrity of the global service information: invalid service information may mislead clients into inappropriate services and may allow attackers to forge server signatures. Clients should accept global service information only from the Global Handle Registry and check its integrity on each update.

For efficiency reasons handle servers do not generate or return a digital signature for every service response unless a client specifically asks, so clients must explicitly ask for the signature to be sure of data integrity, and may set up a session with the server to encrypt data with a session key.

Privacy: by default most handle data is publicly accessible unless the administrator says otherwise, so administrators must be careful when adding values containing private information, and may mark values readable only by the administrator or store them encrypted. Log files generated by handle servers are another vulnerable point, and operators must protect them carefully.

Caching and proxy servers present themselves as men in the middle and are vulnerable to man-in-the-middle attacks. They are not part of any handle service; they are clients of the Handle System, and their service responses cannot be authenticated by the Handle System protocol, so the trust between a client and its immediate proxy has to be set up independently. Log information gathered at proxies often contains highly sensitive personal information and should be carefully guarded. Cache contents are an attractive target, because an attack on the cache can reveal private data or information a user believes they have removed, so cache contents should be protected as sensitive information.

Mirroring sites can lag behind each other, so clients should send time-sensitive requests to the primary site, each mirroring site must follow the same security procedures to ensure data integrity, and software tools may be applied to keep mirroring sites consistent. Denial of service attacks apply as they do to any public service: no general solutions are available in today's technology, and stateless cookies are one means of mitigating some of the effects on hosts that perform authentication, integrity and encryption services.
sections.plainLanguage: The weak spots are the places where trust is taken on faith: the registry that points clients at the right service, the caching proxies that sit in between, and the log files that record who looked up what. The memo tells each of these to be treated as sensitive.
